title: HE HAD JUST MARRIED A WIFE—SO HE TURNED DOWN THE KINGDOM’S INVITATION. WHAT DID JESUS SEE IN THAT EXCUSE?
paragraphs: HE HAD JUST MARRIED A WIFE—SO HE TURNED DOWN THE KINGDOM’S INVITATION. WHAT DID JESUS SEE IN THAT EXCUSE?

Three men were invited to a magnificent banquet. One had property. Another had possessions. The third had someone he loved. But beneath their perfectly reasonable excuses, Jesus exposed a terrifying possibility: You can be surrounded by God's blessings and still refuse the God who gave them.
There is something deeply unsettling about the third man in Jesus' parable.
He wasn't caught stealing.
He wasn't worshiping an idol made of stone.
He wasn't living in some scandalous affair.
He had just gotten married.
And somehow, that became his reason for refusing an invitation to a great banquet.
Read that again.
A man had entered one of life's most beautiful, God-given relationships, and Jesus included his response among the excuses of people who would not come.
Why?
Why would Jesus deliberately mention marriage?
Was He suggesting that marriage is a distraction from God? Was He condemning a husband for wanting to spend time with his new wife? Was there something sinful about beginning a family?
No.
And that is precisely why this parable should make us uncomfortable.
Because Jesus wasn't exposing something obviously wicked.
He was exposing something far more difficult to recognize.
The frightening possibility that something genuinely good can become the very thing we use to keep God at a distance.
And before you decide this story is about somebody else, consider something.
What if you have never rejected Jesus with your mouth...
But have been declining His invitation with your priorities for years?
What if your greatest spiritual danger isn't the sin you are ashamed of, but the blessing you have quietly placed above the One who gave it?
Stay with this story.
Because the man who had just married a wife may reveal something about your own heart that you never expected to see.
And the ending of this banquet is not merely a warning.
It is one of the most astonishing pictures of grace Jesus ever painted.
Jesus told this parable while dining in the house of a prominent Pharisee.
The atmosphere was already uncomfortable.

Religious leaders were watching Him closely. Jesus had challenged their understanding of the Sabbath, confronted their desire for places of honor, and taught His host to extend hospitality to people who could not repay him.
Then someone at the table declared:
“Blessed is he that shall eat bread in the kingdom of God.” (Luke 14:15, KJV)
It sounded beautiful.
Religious.
Respectable.
The kind of statement that would make everyone around the table nod in agreement.
But Jesus knew that talking about the kingdom of God and responding to its King were not the same thing.
So He told them a story.
“A certain man made a great supper, and bade many: And sent his servant at supper time to say to them that were bidden, Come; for all things are now ready.” (Luke 14:16–17, KJV)
Imagine the scene.
The tables have been prepared.
The food is ready.
The host has spared no effort.
The invitations have already gone out.
And now the servant arrives with the announcement everyone should have been waiting to hear.
Come.
Everything is ready.

In the social setting reflected by the parable, an invitation could be followed by a summons when the meal was prepared. Jesus' story emphasizes that these guests were already invited before the servant announced that the banquet was ready.
They were not being asked to organize the celebration.
They were not being told to purchase admission.
They were not being required to prepare the feast.
The host had already done what was necessary.
All they needed to do was come.
And that is where the story becomes painfully revealing.
“And they all with one consent began to make excuse.” (Luke 14:18, KJV)
All of them.
Different circumstances.
Different explanations.
The same refusal.
One man said he had bought a piece of land and needed to inspect it.
Another said he had purchased five yoke of oxen and needed to test them.
Then came the third.
“And another said, I have married a wife, and therefore I cannot come.” (Luke 14:20, KJV)
There it is.
One sentence.
No apology.
No promise to come later.
Just a declaration.
I have married a wife.
Therefore, I cannot come.
And the question is unavoidable.
Why did Jesus include this particular excuse?
To understand its force, we need to look carefully at the language Jesus' audience heard.

Luke's Gospel was written in Greek. Although Jesus likely taught in Aramaic in many everyday settings, we do not possess an original Aramaic transcript of this parable. The Greek text is our earliest surviving textual witness to the wording of Luke's account.
The relevant Greek reads:
γυναῖκα ἔγημα, καὶ διὰ τοῦτο οὐ δύναμαι ἐλθεῖν.
Transliteration: Gynaika egēma, kai dia touto ou dynamai elthein.
A close translation is:
“I have married a wife, and for this reason I am not able to come.”
Notice the expression:
οὐ δύναμαι — ou dynamai.
“I am not able.”
“I cannot.”
The speaker presents his marriage as the reason he is unable to attend.
But Jesus does not tell us that the man's wife was ill.
He does not say she was in danger.
He does not describe a family emergency.
He simply gives us a man who has married and now declares that he cannot come.
The difference matters.
Jesus does not condemn the man for loving his wife.
The man's own explanation becomes part of a larger picture of invited guests who place other concerns ahead of the banquet.
The first man has land.
The second has oxen.
The third has a marriage.
Property.
Work.
Family.
Things that can be legitimate gifts of God.
And yet all three become reasons to refuse.
Perhaps this is where the story begins to find us.
Because most of us would never openly say, “Jesus, I don't want You.”
We say something that sounds much more reasonable.
“Lord, once my business is stable.”
“Lord, after the children grow older.”
“Lord, when this relationship is settled.”
“Lord, when I finish building the life I've been working so hard to create.”
“Lord, when I have more time.”
And somehow, the years pass.
The business grows.
The children get older.
The responsibilities multiply.
The calendar fills.
The house becomes more comfortable.
But the heart becomes strangely unfamiliar with the presence of God.
Not because God has stopped calling.
But because we have become extraordinarily skilled at explaining why we cannot answer.
There is an important detail here that deserves careful attention.
Under the law of Moses, a newly married man received a special consideration.
Deuteronomy 24:5 says:

“When a man hath taken a new wife, he shall not go out to war, neither shall he be charged with any business: but he shall be free at home one year, and shall cheer up his wife which he hath taken.” (KJV)
In the Hebrew text, the expression נָקִי יִהְיֶה לְבֵיתוֹ (naqi yihyeh leveito) conveys that he is to be free for his household.
The command protected a newly established marriage from certain public obligations, especially military service.
God was not treating marriage as unimportant.
He was honoring it.
He recognized the importance of a husband being present with his new wife.
And this is exactly why we must interpret Jesus' parable carefully.
Deuteronomy 24:5 does not say that a newly married man must decline a banquet invitation.
The passage concerns exemption from war and specified obligations, not a general prohibition against attending meals or accepting invitations.
Some interpreters see a possible echo of that law in the man's excuse. But Luke does not explicitly identify Deuteronomy 24:5 as the reason for his refusal.
We should not claim more than Scripture tells us.
What we can say is that Jesus deliberately places marriage alongside property and business as something an invited guest uses to justify his absence.
The problem is not that marriage is unholy.
The problem is that the invitation is refused.
And now we reach a truth that can expose even the most respectable Christian life.
A gift from God becomes spiritually dangerous when we begin treating it as a reason to neglect God Himself.
Think about that husband.
He may have loved his wife deeply.
He may have dreamed of building a peaceful home.
He may have wanted to provide, protect, and enjoy the beautiful life ahead of them.
None of those desires is inherently sinful.
But if a good thing becomes the ultimate thing, it begins demanding the loyalty that belongs to God.
This is not only a marriage problem.
It can happen with children.
With careers.
With ministry.
With financial security.
With education.
With the desire to be respected.
Even with the longing to finally be happy.
A parent can become so consumed with providing for the family that prayer disappears from the home.
A husband and wife can spend years building a comfortable life together while slowly becoming strangers to the Word of God.
A Christian can become so busy serving in church that personal communion with Christ is neglected.
Someone can work tirelessly to obtain the very blessings they once prayed for, only to discover that those blessings now occupy nearly every waking thought.
And perhaps the saddest part is that none of it necessarily looks rebellious.
From the outside, it may look responsible.
Successful.
Admirable.
Even blessed.
But the soul knows when something is missing.
You can sit in a beautiful home and feel spiritually empty.
You can sleep beside someone you love and still feel distant from the Lord.
You can provide everything your children need materially while failing to show them what it looks like to depend upon Jesus.
You can be admired by people and still carry the quiet conviction that God has been receiving whatever time is left over.
And one day, you may realize that you did not abandon your faith in one dramatic moment.
You simply kept postponing the invitation.
One reasonable excuse at a time.
But there is another side to this that must not be overlooked.
Jesus is not calling husbands to abandon their wives.
He is not calling parents to neglect their children.
He is not telling believers to despise work, reject responsibility, or treat ordinary human relationships as obstacles to holiness.
Scripture commands husbands to love their wives as Christ loved the church (Ephesians 5:25).
It calls believers to provide for their households (1 Timothy 5:8).
It teaches that marriage is honorable (Hebrews 13:4).
And it tells Christians to do their work heartily, as unto the Lord (Colossians 3:23).
The biblical answer is not to stop loving your family.
It is to love your family under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
Not to abandon your responsibilities.
But to fulfill them in obedience to Him.
Not to choose between a godly marriage and a faithful walk with Christ.
But to recognize that marriage itself finds its proper place when Christ is Lord.
Jesus said:
“But seek ye first the kingdom of God, and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you.” (Matthew 6:33, KJV)
Seek first.
Not seek only.
Not neglect everything else.
Seek first.
Because when Jesus occupies His rightful place, every other relationship can be understood in the light of His truth.
Your spouse was never meant to be your savior.
Your children were never meant to become your entire identity.
Your career was never meant to provide the ultimate security of your soul.
And your accomplishments were never meant to answer the deepest question of your existence.
Only Christ can bear that weight.
And if you have been placing that weight upon someone you love, you may be exhausting both yourself and them.
No husband can redeem his wife.
No wife can cleanse her husband's sins.
No child can give a parent eternal life.
No amount of success can reconcile a sinner to God.
Only Jesus can do that.
And He did not accomplish it by offering advice from a comfortable distance.
He came into our broken world.
He bore our sin.
He died on the cross.
He rose again.
And through Him, sinners are called to repentance, forgiveness, and reconciliation with God.
This is why the banquet matters so much.
The invitation is not merely about attending a pleasant religious event.
Within the parable's setting, the great supper points toward participation in the blessing of God's kingdom.
The host's invitation reveals generosity.
The guests' excuses reveal refusal.
And what happens next reveals a grace that should leave every reader speechless.
When the servant returns with the excuses, the master of the house becomes angry.
That detail is important.
Grace is not indifference.
God's invitation is not something to treat as worthless.
Refusing a gracious summons is serious.
But listen to what the master commands:
“Go out quickly into the streets and lanes of the city, and bring in hither the poor, and the maimed, and the halt, and the blind.” (Luke 14:21, KJV)
The poor.
The disabled.
The people society might overlook.
The people who could not offer the host impressive connections or repay him with another magnificent banquet.
These are the very kinds of people Jesus had already told His host to invite in Luke 14:12–14.
And now they stand at the center of the story.
Imagine hearing that invitation if you had spent your life being treated as though you did not belong.
Imagine having nothing impressive to bring.
No expensive gift.
No prestigious title.
No ability to repay the host.
And suddenly someone comes into your street and announces that a place has been prepared.
You are invited.
Not because you can enrich the host.
Not because you have earned a position.
But because he has chosen to extend his generosity.
And then comes another astonishing detail.
The servant reports that the master's command has been carried out.
Yet there is still room.
So the master says:
“Go out into the highways and hedges, and compel them to come in, that my house may be filled.” (Luke 14:23, KJV)
The Greek expression ἀνάγκασον εἰσελθεῖν (anankason eiselthein) can be translated “compel them to come in.”
That word has sometimes been misused to justify religious coercion.
But such a reading is contrary to the character of the invitation in this parable.

The scene is one of extending hospitality to people who might never imagine themselves welcome at such a feast. In this context, the language naturally communicates an urgent, insistent invitation, not a command for Christians to force people into faith.
The master wants his house filled.
Those who seemed least likely to receive such an invitation are being summoned.
And here the Gospel begins to shine through the story with extraordinary beauty.
The kingdom of God is not a private banquet reserved for people who have successfully disguised their brokenness.
Jesus came calling sinners to repentance.
He welcomed the despised.
He touched the unclean.
He ate with tax collectors.
He showed mercy to those whom religious society had learned to dismiss.
And He did not merely offer them a better reputation.
He offered them Himself.
This is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
We are not saved because our past is respectable.
We are not saved because our marriages are perfect.
We are not saved because we have never disappointed God.
We are saved by grace through faith in Jesus Christ, not by our own works (Ephesians 2:8–9).
And the grace that saves us also calls us into a new life of obedience.
Maybe you know what it feels like to be the person standing outside.
Maybe your marriage has not become the beautiful story you imagined.
Maybe there have been arguments you never thought you would have.
Promises that were broken.
Conversations that ended in silence.
Nights when two people lay in the same bed but felt miles apart.
Maybe you have been divorced.
Maybe you have buried the person you thought you would grow old beside.
Maybe you are unmarried and exhausted from hearing people speak as though your life will only begin when someone chooses you.
Maybe you have been betrayed.
Maybe you were the one who betrayed someone else's trust.
Maybe your family looks respectable on Sunday while quietly falling apart behind closed doors.
Listen carefully.
The banquet invitation is not reserved for people whose lives turned out beautifully.
The Gospel is for sinners who need a Savior.
For people who have failed.
For people who are tired of pretending.
For people who have made idols of good things.
For people who have wasted years.
For people who are finally willing to admit that they cannot save themselves.
And that includes the person reading this with tears in their eyes.
But we must also hear the warning.
Because Jesus did not end the parable by saying that every invited guest eventually arrived.
He ended with these words:
“For I say unto you, That none of those men which were bidden shall taste of my supper.” (Luke 14:24, KJV)
That is a sobering conclusion.
The original guests were invited.
They were summoned.
They offered their excuses.
And they missed the banquet.
We should not soften Jesus' warning until it loses its meaning.
His invitation is gracious, but it must not be treated with contempt.
The kingdom is not something we can indefinitely postpone while assuming that our own preferred schedule will determine the terms of our response.
There is urgency in the words:
“Come; for all things are now ready.”
And this brings us back to the newly married man.
What became of him?
Jesus does not tell us.
We do not know his name.
We do not know his wife's name.
We do not know what happened in their home afterward.
We do not know whether he ever regretted his refusal.
And that silence is powerful.
Because the point of the story is not to reconstruct his biography.
It is to examine our own response.
Maybe his excuse sounds familiar because yours has been so similar.
You love your family.
You work hard.
You are trying to build a future.
You want to be responsible.
You want to be happy.
But somewhere along the way, Jesus has become Someone you intend to take more seriously someday.
Someday when the bills are paid.
Someday when the marriage is easier.
Someday when the children are independent.
Someday when the business is secure.
Someday when you have finished enjoying the life you have built.
But what if the deepest tragedy is not that you have too little time?
What if it is that you have given the center of your heart to something that was never meant to occupy God's throne?
And what if Jesus is not asking you to destroy the good things in your life?
What if He is calling you to stop asking those good things to be your god?
Perhaps the most loving thing you could do for your spouse today is to repent of making your marriage your ultimate source of meaning.
Perhaps the most loving thing you could do for your children is to let them see you humbly following Jesus.
Perhaps the most important thing you could do for your future is to surrender the illusion that you control it.
And perhaps the most honest prayer you can pray tonight is not a polished religious speech.
Maybe it is simply this:
“Lord Jesus, I have been making excuses.
I have been calling my distractions responsibilities.
I have been enjoying Your gifts while neglecting Your presence.
I have been trying to build a life that feels complete without surrendering every part of it to You.
Forgive me.
Show me what I have placed above You.
Teach me to love my family without making them my god.
Teach me to work faithfully without worshiping success.
Teach me to receive Your blessings with gratitude instead of allowing them to rule my heart.
I cannot save myself.
I need Your mercy.
I believe You died for sinners and rose again.
I turn to You.
Be Lord of my life.
And let my home, my relationships, my work, and my future belong to You.
Amen.”
If that prayer expressed something you have been struggling to admit, don't rush past this moment.
You do not have to share the details of your private pain publicly.
But perhaps you can take one small, honest step.

And if Christ has already been teaching you to surrender something you once placed above Him, consider sharing a little of that testimony. Someone else may need to know that repentance is not the end of hope.
It can be the beginning of restoration.
There is something else I want you to remember.
The people who first heard this parable were sitting at a meal, speaking about the blessing of eating in God's kingdom.
They were physically close to Jesus.
They could hear His voice.
They could listen to His teaching.
Yet Jesus still warned them about refusing the invitation.
Religious proximity is not the same as surrender.
Knowing the language of faith is not the same as trusting Christ.
Being familiar with Scripture is not the same as obeying the Lord Scripture reveals.
You can discuss the kingdom and still resist the King.
You can admire Jesus and still refuse to follow Him.
You can spend years around Christian things while keeping certain rooms of your heart locked.
But the call of the Gospel is not merely to become a more religious person.
It is to repent and believe in Jesus Christ.
To receive His grace.
To trust His finished work.
To follow Him as Lord.
And to let that faith reshape the ordinary places where life actually happens.
Your kitchen.
Your workplace.
Your marriage.
Your finances.
Your private thoughts.
Your decisions when nobody is watching.
Your conversations when you are angry.
Your willingness to forgive.
Your response when God calls you to obey and obedience becomes costly.
This is where discipleship becomes real.
Not merely in the words we post.
But in the lives we live.
And if this message has convicted you, consider what might happen if someone else heard it at exactly the right moment.
Perhaps there is a friend who has been drifting away from Jesus while building a successful career.
Perhaps there is a couple who needs to remember that Christ belongs at the center of their home.
Perhaps there is a parent carrying the exhaustion of providing for everyone while quietly starving spiritually.
Perhaps there is someone who believes their past has disqualified them from God's mercy.
Not simply to spread another religious post.
Because a single emotional moment is not the same as a life of discipleship.
We need the Word of God beyond the moment when we feel moved.
We need to keep learning.
Keep praying.
Keep repenting.
Keep growing.
Keep returning to Christ.
That is part of the reason Gospel Warrior exists.
We want to keep bringing biblical truth into homes, marriages, struggles, and ordinary days.
We want to reach people who feel forgotten.
We want to encourage believers who are weary.
We want to help those who are hungry for Scripture move beyond inspirational quotations into deeper understanding of God's Word.
And we want this work to continue growing.
These resources are meant to help people study, reflect, mature in faith, and remain grounded in biblical truth.
Scripture teaches:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” (2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV)
That is the spirit in which we invite you.
Not through guilt.
Not through fear.
And not because giving to this particular ministry is a biblical requirement.

Rather, if you believe this work is helping people encounter the truth of Scripture, you can voluntarily make it part of your personal giving and support for Gospel ministry, according to your convictions and ability.
These products can serve as everyday reminders of faith, encouragement, and opportunities for Gospel-centered conversations.
It is the opportunity to help make Christ known.
It is not a substitute for worship, obedience, or personal discipleship.
It is simply an opportunity to stand alongside a ministry whose mission you believe in.
Keep reading.
Keep studying.
Keep sharing.
Keep growing in the grace and knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ.
No one should ever feel that they must pay to be welcomed into a community centered on the Gospel.
The invitation of Christ is not for sale.
And that brings us back to the banquet.
Because after all these words, all these Scriptures, and all these questions, there is one truth I do not want you to forget.
The man who had just married a wife had something beautiful in his life.
But he allowed that beautiful thing to become his reason for not coming.
And we must ask ourselves whether we have done the same.
Have we made a blessing into an excuse?
Have we allowed the life God gave us to become a distraction from the God who gave us life?
Have we become so occupied with the gifts that we no longer listen for the Giver?
The answer is not to despise what God has given.
It is to surrender it to Him.
And if you recognize yourself in this parable, do not turn conviction into despair.
Let it lead you to repentance.
The same Jesus who warned about refusing the banquet is the Savior who gave His life for sinners.
He did not come merely to expose what was wrong with us.
He came to accomplish what we could never accomplish for ourselves.
At the cross, our sin was not ignored.
Its seriousness was revealed.
And in the death and resurrection of Jesus Christ, God's saving grace was gloriously displayed.
That is why our theme is not simply scandal.
It is From Scandal to Grace.
Not because sin does not matter.
But because Jesus Christ is mighty to save.
He can forgive the guilty.
Restore the repentant.
Heal what has been wounded.
Transform what has been surrendered.
And give eternal life to those who trust in Him.
So before you close this article, ask yourself one final question.
Not whether you are married.
Not whether you own property.
Not whether you have responsibilities.
Not whether your life looks successful.
Ask yourself this:
If Jesus is calling me to surrender my life to Him, what excuse am I still holding in my hands?
And then remember the words that began the parable.
“Come; for all things are now ready.”
The banquet was prepared before the guests were summoned.
And in the Gospel, salvation rests not upon our ability to make ourselves worthy, but upon the finished work of Jesus Christ.
Come to Him in repentance and faith.
Not when your life finally looks perfect.
Not when you have collected enough religious achievements.
Not when you have successfully repaired every broken piece of your past.
Come because you need the Savior.
Come because His mercy is greater than your ability to rescue yourself.
Come because tomorrow is not promised.
Come because Christ is worthy of more than the leftovers of your life.
Your testimony may encourage another person to stop postponing the response they know they need to make.
The third man had a wife.
The first had a field.
The second had oxen.
But the tragedy was never that they had something good.
It was that, when the invitation came, they would not come.
Do not spend your whole life thanking God for the blessings He gave you, only to discover that you kept using those very blessings as reasons to stay away from Him.
